speaker: Anaëlle Touré
title: The Rising Role of Just Transition and Labor in Decarbonization Plans: Evidence from NDCs
abstract:
As the energy transition accelerates, concerns about its distributional consequences in labor markets have moved to the center of climate policy debates. Governments have increasingly responded by adopting Just Transition frameworks and labor market programs aimed at protecting workers in affected industries. Yet comparable cross-country data remain scarce, leaving limited evidence on the extent of these provisions and the ways in which they are designed.
This paper constructs a novel, large-scale dataset capturing the labor and social policy content of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) submitted under the Paris Agreement across three submission cycles (2015–2025), covering up to 194 countries. Because NDCs are unstructured policy documents, we develop a coding pipeline combining large language model annotation with targeted keyword searches validated against human-coded data. The resulting dataset includes 96 variables per country-cycle observation based on policy categories.
We document three main findings. First, references to Just Transition and employment have expanded rapidly across NDC cycles. Second, despite this convergence in language, countries display substantial heterogeneity in the policy areas and target groups they emphasize. Third, cluster analysis reveals four distinct policy-mix typologies that vary in the depth and the focus of policy engagement. One cluster shows persistently lower commitment, while the others are oriented toward industrial policy, social policy, or comprehensive high-ambition approaches. Over time, countries tend to shift toward higher-commitment typologies. We then provide exploratory evidence on the determinants of high-commitment policy portfolios. Commitment is generally higher in more democratic regimes, although this relationship appears to be moderated by fossil fuel production: among democracies, higher levels of fossil fuel production are associated with a lower likelihood of belonging to the high-commitment cluster.
